subject: ss-critical-care
title: Arrhythmias and acute cardiac care in the ICU

steps.tx: New **atrial fibrillation**, a chaotic atrial rhythm, is often driven by sepsis, withdrawal, or stretch of the atrium. The unstable patient is electrically cardioverted, and the stable patient is rate controlled. Anticoagulation is chosen from stroke risk and bleeding risk, and it is not a reflex heparin infusion. Treating the rhythm and leaving the sepsis in place does not remove the trigger.

vis.alt: Pulmonary vein foci, chaotic atrial wavelets, a left atrial appendage thrombus, and a rhythm strip with no P waves.
vis.caption: Pulmonary-vein triggers, chaotic wavelets, appendage thrombus, and an irregular strip with no P waves. The drawing does not show a rate target or an anticoagulation score. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: **Amiodarone** is the usual rhythm drug when the heart is structurally abnormal. A fast infusion can drop the blood pressure. Thyroid disease and lung toxicity from a long course can outlast the ICU stay, so the drug is not a casual discharge prescription. The acute rhythm is the indication, and a stop date is part of the order.

steps.tx: **Synchronised cardioversion** is for an unstable tachyarrhythmia that still has a pulse, because the shock is timed off the QRS. Pulseless ventricular tachycardia and **ventricular fibrillation** are defibrillated, and they are not synchronised. A synchronised shock that waits for a QRS will not fire when there is no organised complex.

left.title: Shock with a pulse
points: The shock is timed off the QRS
The patient is unstable but perfusing

right.title: No pulse
points: Waiting for a QRS will not fire

steps.tx: **Torsades de pointes** is a twisting polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. It is treated with **magnesium sulfate** 2 g even when the serum magnesium is normal. Potassium is corrected, the QT drug is stopped, and pacing or isoproterenol is used when the rhythm is pause dependent. A normal magnesium result is not a reason to withhold that dose.

vis.caption: A wide, irregular, polymorphic ventricular rhythm. The headers are rate, lead, and paper speed only, with no name. It does not show the QT interval, a magnesium level, or a pacing spike. Credit: Panthro, via Wikimedia Commons.

steps.tx: **Transvenous pacing** is for symptomatic bradycardia that has not responded to atropine or a chronotropic infusion, and it is also for overdrive pacing of recurrent pause-dependent torsades. Asynchronous pacing that lands on a T wave can start ventricular fibrillation. Capture and the sensing threshold are checked before the team leaves the bedside.

steps.tx: **Acute decompensated heart failure** with pulmonary oedema is treated with non-invasive ventilation, a nitrate when the blood pressure allows it, and a diuretic. Inotropes are for low-output shock, and they are not for every wet patient. A wet patient with a safe blood pressure does not need an inotrope because the radiograph is white.

steps.tx: A **hypertensive emergency** is organ injury, and it is not a blood pressure number by itself. Encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema, an acute coronary syndrome, dissection, or eclampsia is the injury that defines it. The pressure is lowered in a controlled way. It is not normalised within minutes, except in dissection and eclampsia, where the fall is faster.

steps.tx: **ST elevation** myocardial infarction in the ICU is still an indication for immediate reperfusion. A new murmur after infarction can be a mechanical complication: septal rupture, **papillary muscle** rupture, or free-wall rupture. Those lesions need a surgeon or a device. A higher nitrate dose is not the treatment for a ruptured muscle.
